description.narrative:
Den nuvarande fasen av "Open Fun Football Schools Project" och det sektorsövergripande nätverket för social prevention kommer att genomföras under 2024-2028 av Cross Culture Project Association (CCPA), en dansk civilsamhällesorganisation, i partnerskap med Moldaviens fotbollsförbund (FMF) och Association for Participatory Criminal Justice (AJPP).
Interventionen bygger på plattformar och tillvägagångssätt som utvecklats i Moldavien av de programpartner som stöds av Sverige sedan 2009. Dessutom bygger det på en studieresa till Danmark, med syftet att undersöka filosofin bakom det effektiva danska SSP-initiativet som syftar till att skapa formaliserade och lämpliga sektorsövergripande ramverk för skolor, socialförvaltning och polis i syfte att förebygga och följa upp barn och ungdomars problem relaterade till brottslighet. Projektet är strategiskt placerat för att främja samarbete och skapa synergier med General Inspectorate Police's Community Security Councils. Genom ett nära samarbete med dessa råd kommer projektet att stärka kapaciteten hos lokala civilsamhällesorganisationer och CSP-team att aktivt delta i frågor som rör inrikesfrågor, säkerhet och migration. Denna samarbetsstrategi är utformad för att berika dialogen mellan det civila samhället, nationella myndigheter och medborgare, vilket främjar en sammanhängande och säker samhällsstruktur. Syftet med OFFS+CSP-initiativet kommer att gå utöver dess ursprungliga koncept och bredda insatserna för att utveckla en hållbar mekanism för sektorsövergripande samarbete som arbetar för att förebygga eller minska förekomsten av sociala frågor, problem eller risker.
Projektet kommer att ta itu med ungdomsbrottslighet och skolors säkerhet genom att införa reparativa metoder som är anpassade till de särskilda förhållandena vid utbildningsinstitutioner i Moldavien. Genom att främja det reparativa tillvägagångssättet kommer det att skapa ett prejudikat för tidigt ingripande för att hantera konflikter och skadligt beteende på ett sätt som går utöver det traditionella tillvägagångssättet, vilket hjälper till att bygga samhällen som är säkrare, mer sammanhållna och inriktade på att förebygga konflikter. Dessa metoder kommer inte bara att förändra sättet att reagera på konflikter och säkerhetsproblem, utan också odla en kultur av ansvar, ömsesidig förståelse och försoning, vilket får en positiv inverkan på hela samhället. Hittills har mer än 93 000 barn (54 % flickor), 12 000 föräldrar och 2 700 frivilliga ledare och tränare, 77 fotbollsklubbar och mer än 650 daghem, skolor och idrottsskolor i Moldavien deltagit i projektet. Dessutom har 470 lokala poliser i distrikten varit involverade som intressenter i Open Fun Football School-projektet och utvecklat relevanta barnskyddsåtgärder inom Sport + School + Police-aktiviteterna. Projektbudgeten för hela projektet som pågår i 12 distrikt, inklusive Transnistrienregionen och Gagauzia, från april 2024 - 31 december 2028 är 24 922 693 SEK. Sida kommer att stödja bidraget med ett totalt belopp på 22.00.000 SEK, vilket motsvarar 88% av de totala projektkostnaderna.

The current phase of the 'Open Fun Football Schools Project’ and the Cross-sector Social Prevention network will be implemented in 2024-2028 by Cross Culture Project Association (CCPA), a Danish civil society organization, in partnership with the Moldovan Football Federation (FMF) and Association for Participatory Criminal Justice (AJPP).
The intervention is built on platforms and approaches developed in Moldova by the program partners supported by Sweden since 2009. Further, it builds on a study tour to Denmark, with the purpose to examine the philosophy behind the impactful Danish SSP initiative that aims to create formalized and appropriate cross-sector frameworks for schools, social administration, and police with a view to preventing and following up on children and young people's problems related to crime. The project is strategically positioned to foster cooperation and generate synergy with the General Inspectorate Police's Community Security Councils. Through close collaboration with these councils, project will bolster the capacities of local CSOs and CSP-teams to actively participate in matters concerning home affairs, security, and migration. This collaborative approach is designed to enrich the dialogue between civil society, national authorities, and citizens, promoting a cohesive and secure community fabric. The purpose of OFFS+CSP-initiative will go beyond its original concept and broaden interventions to develop a sustainable mechanism for cross-sector collaboration that works to prevent or reduce the occurrence of social issues, problems, or risks.
The project will address juvenile delinquency and schools’ safety by introducing restorative practices adapted to the specifics of educational institutions in the Republic of Moldova. By promoting the restorative approach, it will set a precedent for early intervention in addressing conflicts and harmful behavior in a way that exceeds the traditional approach, helping to build communities that are safer, more cohesive, and oriented towards preventing conflicts. These practices will not only transform the way of responding to conflicts and safety problems, but also cultivate a culture of responsibility, mutual understanding, and reconciliation, having a positive impact on the whole society. So far, the project has accommodated more than 93,000 children (54% girls), 12,000 parents and 2,700 voluntary leaders and coaches, 77 football clubs and more than 650 kindergarten, schools, and sport schools across Moldova. Furthermore, 470 community police officers in the districts have been involved as stakeholder in the Open Fun Football School project, developing relevant child protection measures within the Sport + School + Police activities. The project budget for the entire project running in 12 districts, including Transnistria region and Gagauzia, from April 2024 – 31 December 2028 is 24.922.693 SEK. Sida will support the contribution with a total amount of 22.00.000 SEK, which corresponds to 88% of the total project costs.

Project will contribute to facilitating:
A civil society network that engages local stakeholders in organizing inter-community-based children grassroots football across political and social divides Permanent cooperation between sport school social police (CSP) Problem-oriented bottom-up approach to achieve security and social prevention initiatives Respect for good governance, human rights, equality and diversity
The ultimate goal and impact of the project will be to foster inter- and intra-community relations and bottom-up civil society initiatives that contribute to peaceful co-existence, child protection, gender equality, good governance and public security.

sector.narrative: Civilian peace-building, conflict prevention and resolution

description.narrative:
2024: During the 2024 inception phase of the OFFSCSP initiative in Moldova, significant progress was made in establishing a collaborative framework for addressing juvenile delinquency and promoting social inclusion through sport and cross-sectoral coordination. Led by Cross Cultures, in partnership with the Association for Participatory Criminal Justice (AJPP) and the Football Federation of Moldova (FMF), the project aimed to foster resilience among at-risk youth and strengthen community-level responses.
One of the most notable expected results was the establishment of formal cooperation agreements between AJPP and two key government bodies: the Ministry of Education and Research and the General Police Inspectorate. These agreements marked an important step in operationalizing Moldovas multidisciplinary response mechanisms (EMD teams) for children in conflict with the law. AJPP also continued its long-standing collaboration with the Ministry of Justice and its subordinate bodies, including the National Probation Inspectorate and the National Administration of Penitentiaries, ensuring strong integration of justice-sector perspectives.
In parallel, AJPP led a thorough evaluation of Moldovas national education curriculum, aiming to identify strengths and gaps in how delinquency prevention is addressed. This assessment included a desk review of legal frameworks and targeted interviews with education officials. A comparative analysis with the Danish prevention model was also initiated, providing valuable benchmarks for future policy recommendations.
Capacity building was another core achievement. AJPP conducted four regional roundtables, engaging 92 professionals across 10 districts, from fields such as education, law enforcement, mental health, and probation. These roundtables served as platforms for dialogue and revealed several unexpected insights. Professionals highlighted that while a multidisciplinary mechanism exists, actual cooperation is often fragmented, with many actors still working in silos. The absence of psychologists in schools, overlapping classifications of at-risk children, and lack of training in school mediation were identified as systemic weaknesses needing urgent attention.
A particularly impactful and unexpected result emerged from the pilot school mediation training held in Orhei, where 20 students and several educators were introduced to peer-to-peer conflict resolution techniques. The strong interest and engagement from participants underscored a critical unmet need for such programs in schools. AJPP responded by developing a practical toolkit on school mediation to support the trainees in applying their skills in real-world contexts.
An important highlight of the inception phase was the study visit to Sweden and Denmark, where Moldovan stakeholders observed how Scandinavian countries coordinate child protection efforts across sectors. This exposure helped shape Moldovas future strategy by reinforcing the importance of localized, family-centered interventions and continuous professional development. Participants returned with renewed commitment to decentralizing services and empowering frontline professionals.
Meanwhile, the Football Federation of Moldova (FMF) played a crucial role in facilitating the Open Fun Football Schools (OFFS), which serve as inclusive, community-based platforms where sports and social development intersect. FMF trained new coaches and local leaders in child protection and community engagement, using football as a medium to build trust, encourage teamwork, and reduce social risks among youth. Their efforts bridged collaboration between schools, social services, law enforcement, and civil society at the local level.
Through FMF's contributions, the project not only reached vulnerable children with structured recreational activities but also promoted positive role models and safe environments that can deter youth from engaging in delinquent behavior. Their involvement demonstrated how sport can be harnessed not just for physical development, but as a powerful tool for social change and community cohesion.
As a whole, the inception phase delivered key foundational results: the formation of institutional alliances, generation of actionable data, implementation of pilot trainings, and growing public and institutional interest in preventive and rehabilitative approaches for at-risk youth.
The learnings from 2024 have informed the planning of expanded activities for 2025, including broader school mediation training, the development of specialized probation programs, legislative review support, and continued investment in intersectoral collaboration. Together, AJPP and FMF have laid the groundwork for a multi-year effort that is responsive, inclusive, and grounded in both local realities and international best practices.
Update of results 2025:
The programme continued to contribute to the promotion of peaceful coexistence, social inclusion, child protection, gender equality, and cross-sector social prevention mechanisms in Moldova, including Transnistria and Gagauzia. The activities implemented throughout 2025 reflected alignment with Moldovas EU accession priorities, particularly under Chapter 23 (Judiciary and Fundamental Rights) and Chapter 24 (Justice, Freedom and Security), as well as broader rule of law and child protection reforms.
During 2025, the programme achieved significant results both in relation to planned objectives and through several positive developments that emerged during implementation. Under the FMF/OFFS component, substantial outreach and mobilisation activities were implemented through football-based community engagement. Twelve Open Fun Football Schools of six-day duration were organised across Moldova, including in Transnistria and Gagauzia, engaging 2,406 children, of whom 55% were girls. The activities promoted interaction among Moldovan, Transnistrian, Gagauzian and Ukrainian children and volunteers, contributing to social cohesion and confidence-building across communities. The programme also succeeded in mobilising and training over 320 volunteers from different professional sectors, including education, sports, police and social services, thereby strengthening local cross-sector collaboration.
The programme further strengthened cross-sector cooperation through continued collaboration between FMF and the General Police Inspectorate, marking the tenth consecutive year of partnership. The project promotes the community policing approach working closely with Swedish Police Autority in Moldova. Police officers, social workers, schools, sports associations and local authorities participated actively in implementation activities. Community police officers co-led activities in all OFFS locations, while thematic seminars and coordination meetings contributed to strengthening preventive and community-oriented approaches. The involvement of social workers and cooperation with the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection further enhanced inclusion of vulnerable children.
The child protection and inclusion dimension of the programme produced important results. Approximately 300 vulnerable children, including refugee children, children with disabilities, children from deprived families and children without parental care, participated in programme activities. Awareness-raising activities linked to international thematic days addressed childrens rights, disability inclusion, healthy lifestyles and environmental responsibility. The programme also strengthened safeguarding approaches through participation in FIFA safeguarding initiatives and utilisation of UEFA child protection resources.
In relation to youth empowerment and gender equality, the programme exceeded traditional participation patterns in grassroots sport. Girls represented more than half of all child participants and volunteers, while girls football tournaments and women-focused football activities contributed to increasing participation and visibility of girls in sport. Approximately 150 young volunteers, youth referees and coaches were engaged in leadership and practical training activities, contributing to skills development and community participation.
Under the CSP component implemented by Association for Participatory Criminal Justice, significant progress was achieved in strengthening institutional capacities and intersectoral coordination for children at risk and children in conflict with the law. Four regional multidisciplinary trainings brought together police officers, probation counsellors, social workers, psychologists and education representatives to strengthen understanding of referral pathways, child-centred approaches and cross-sector case management practices. The programme also contributed to strengthening preventive and rehabilitative approaches within the justice sector. A specialised probation programme for juvenile offenders involved in property-related offences was developed and piloted, while 22 probation counsellors received methodological training for implementation. This contributed to Moldovas broader efforts to strengthen non-custodial and rehabilitative measures consistent with EU and national reform priorities.
Additional activities focused on school mediation and integrity in education. School mediation trainings were organised for students in several regions, while practical educational tools, including mediation cards, were developed and later recommended by the Ministry of Education and Research for educational use. Furthermore, an anti-corruption guide for educational institutions was developed in consultation with relevant national authorities, including the National Anticorruption Centre and the National Integrity Authority.
The programme also generated several positive developments beyond the initial expected outputs. One notable example was the emergence of new cooperation agreements between football clubs from Moldova and Transnistria, reportedly developed indirectly through relationships established during OFFS activities. Although not originally foreseen as a programme output, these partnerships demonstrate broader confidence-building and social cohesion effects.
Another positive outcome was the replication and expansion of school mediation activities by educational institutions independently from the project framework. Following AJPP-supported trainings, the Ion Luca Caragiale Lyceum in Orhei initiated additional mediation activities, reflecting institutional ownership and sustainability potential.
